physical_harm: Two brothers died as a result of the shooting
premeditation_planning: The court found no premeditation or planning
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence proved that there was a scuffle in which the appellant was pinned to the floor and deceased attempted to strangulate the appellant. In the scuffle, appellant may have pulled out his gun and upon seeing the gun, the deceased may have released the appellant and started running upon which the appellant may have fired the shot which hit deceased on back. The shot was fired from a distant range, and the bullet entered the body below the right shoulder and travelled upwards without exiting.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses by noting that PW-3 (Hans Raj) did not specify that the appellant shot him, and that the version of PW-30 (Tarsem Kumar) was doubted due to the bullet entry wound being on the back of the deceased, not the front. The court also found that the testimony of PW-23 (Subhash Chand Mahajan) and PW-27 (Sarover Kumar) about the scuffle was unshaken in cross-examination.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was delivered on 01.09.2010 by the High Court of Delhi, and the Supreme Court decision was on 02.02.2017.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: D Sushil Kumar, S. K. Aggarwal, Aditya Kumar, S. K. Sinha, Arun K. Sinha. Counsel for the State: P. K. Dey, R. K. Verma, Ms. Rashmi Malhotra, Ms. Sadhna Sandhu, B. K. Prasad, Ms. Reena Rai, Ms. Shreyasi Chakraborty, Manish, Mrs. Anil Katiyar.
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Sections 302 and 304 read with Section 34 of IPC. High Court: Conviction under Sections 302 and 304 read with Section 34 of IPC. Supreme Court: Conviction under Section 302 for murder of Kishan Lal is set aside, and conviction under Section 304 is maintained.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant shot the deceased and his brothers during a confrontation, resulting in their deaths, and that the appellant took undue advantage of the situation by using the gun even though the deceased and his brothers were unarmed.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant acted in self-defence, as he was being strangled by the deceased and his brothers during a scuffle, and that the shooting was a result of a sudden fight in the heat of passion, not premeditation.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a person in imminent and reasonable danger of losing their life or limb may use self-defence, even if it results in the death of the assailant, provided it is without premeditation and without taking undue advantage.
precedent_relied_upon: Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab and Another (2010) 2 SCC 333 : [2010] 1 SCR 642
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the appellant was already serving a sentence of 13 years, and the court sentenced him to the period already undergone under Section 304 of the IPC.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered that the appellant acted in self-defence without premeditation and that the shooting occurred in a sudden fight in the heat of passion.
